title: After the Fire, Before a Lease
displayTitle: After the Fire, Before a Lease
subtitle: For renters displaced by Los Angeles's January 2025 fires, finding somewhere to stay left another question: how long could they afford to remain?
excerpt: For renters displaced by Los Angeles's January 2025 fires, finding somewhere to stay left another question: how long could they afford to remain?

content.alt: Aerial view of fire-damaged homes and businesses in Altadena
content.caption: Fire-damaged homes and businesses along Lake Street in Altadena. Added to this article on September 26, 2026; the photograph’s capture date has not been confirmed.

content.text: Even before the Eaton Fire, Chevondolyn had to leave her apartment as she could no longer afford to live there. The mother of two had to vacate her apartment in Santa Clarita and moved in with family members. The January fire struck the community she had recently returned to. In an account released by Union Station Homeless Services in August 2025, the organization explained how she lost all that she had after enduring tough times financially.

Between February 1 and March 30, 2025, USC researchers conducted a survey among 1,360 Los Angeles County residents. Among evacuees who had experienced housing insecurity before the fires, 22 percent had not returned home at the time of the survey, compared to 15 percent of those with secure housing.

A family may need enough bedrooms, a convenient commute to work or a place from where children can continue going to school. Moving farther away changes who can help with child care. Living with relatives provides immediate shelter but leaves the longer-term arrangements uncertain.

While helping refugee families find housing in Long Beach, I had to track bedrooms, income limits, deposits and credit requirements of apartments. I would call the apartments to inquire about the requirements and see how well the listing matched.

This experience made me wary of using a list of available properties as a list of homes where people can move in. A family might be able to afford the monthly rent but require help with the deposit. The apartment may fit in the budget but lack space for the whole family.

In California, the housing department tried to do such matching after the fires. In July, it announced that 141 properties answering its survey of state-funded housing in Los Angeles County identified 723 vacant units available in June. The housing department passed the list to the county to help the displaced residents find housing. Residents still needed to fulfill the required eligibility criteria.

content.alt: Workers at the timber frame of a home under construction on Palm Street in Altadena
content.caption: A home under construction on Palm Street in Altadena, April 30, 2026.

content.text: The count of vacancies did not show how many households were eligible, applied or moved in.

Emergency accommodation helped some of the survivors to start looking for housing. Airbnb.org coordinated with 211 LA to arrange free stays for the fire victims. In a January 29 update, Airbnb announced that over 17,000 people had booked temporary accommodation through the response. This announcement also mentioned funding for extra nights and extensions for people who lost their homes.

In July, LAist reporters, in an article republished by KQED, noted that 211 LA was working with over 3,000 fire-affected households, mostly renters. The executive director of 211 LA, Maribel Marin, said clients were seeing much higher rents for similar housing. The report also mentions the organization's data on over 100 families staying in vehicles. These numbers referred to the people within its service network and not the count of all displaced families in the county.

Union Station Homeless Services described a program for fire victims to cover security deposits, back rent, basic furnishings and motel vouchers, with rental assistance available to households requiring it beyond a month. It mentioned that the program was designed to reduce barriers for people not qualifying for traditional assistance.

content.caption: An image accompanying USHS’s account of its Eaton Fire Housing Assistance Program. The source does not identify the people pictured.

content.text: Door of Hope paired housing assistance with guidance on accessing other resources. In March, Pasadena Community Foundation announced that the organization was providing assistance to families in moving into new apartments, applying for FEMA and insurance and covering costs other sources of assistance left unpaid. The funds also paid for a disaster case manager who could help the families with healthcare, therapy and job searches.

For renters, rebuilding raises another question about return. The replacement building will have an address but its construction alone does not tell when a former tenant can move back and what he or she will pay. Until these details are known, the families have to make decisions about living elsewhere.
For Chevondolyn and other displaced renters, the question remains open after a temporary booking or an approved payment: when the assistance runs out, can they still afford to stay?

reportingNote: The sources were first published between January and August 2025. The two USHS pages show later updates dated October 21, 2025; their current wording has not been checked against a summer 2025 archived version. Chevondolyn's experience comes from USHS's published account, not an interview conducted for The Margins. My housing-search observations come from work with refugee families in Long Beach.
